title: Complexity in practice
sub: Big-O as growth of work, amortization, and what the constraints let you afford
cards/0/body:
The complexity of an algorithm is not its time in seconds. It answers the question “how many times more work is there when the data grows”. We count simple operations — a comparison, an addition, reading an array element — as a function of the input size n and keep the leading term without constants: 3n + 5 is O(n), n²/2 + n is O(n²).

Constants are dropped because for large n the leading term swamps the rest, and the constant itself depends on the CPU and the compiler. The growth does not: for O(n), 10 times more data means 10 times more work; for O(n²), 100 times.

How to read code: loops one after another add up (O(n) + O(n) = O(n)), nested loops multiply. With two inputs, each gets its own letter: a loop over b inside a loop over a is O(n·m), not O(n²). Collapsing n and m into one letter is a common interview mistake.
cards/1/q: What is the complexity of this function? a has length n, b has length m.
cards/1/options/3: O(n·m + m), it cannot be simplified
cards/1/explain: Nested loops multiply: for each of the n elements of a there are m steps over b, n·m in total. The second loop adds m, and n·m + m = m·(n + 1), which is O(n·m): the lower-order term is dropped.
cards/1/wrong/1: There are two inputs and their lengths are unrelated: with n = 10 and m = 10⁶ the work is 10⁷, not 100. Each input gets its own letter.
cards/1/wrong/2: Loops one after another add up. Here the loop over b is nested inside the loop over a, so they multiply.
cards/1/wrong/3: It can be simplified: m ≤ n·m for n ≥ 1, so the lower-order term is dropped — O(n·m).
cards/2/title: Best, average and worst case. Memory
cards/2/body:
The same function runs for different times on different inputs. Linear search for a value (Array.IndexOf, List<T>.Contains): the best case is the value at the front, one comparison; the worst is the value missing, n comparisons; the average, if the value is equally likely to be anywhere, is about n/2. Both average and worst are O(n).

Unless stated otherwise, interviews talk about the worst case: it is a guarantee. “On average” is said explicitly, along with what the average is over. A hash table lookup is O(1) on average over the distribution of keys and O(n) in the worst case; how that happens is in the next lesson.

Memory is part of complexity too. You count extra memory beyond the input: a dictionary of n elements is O(n), a couple of variables is O(1). Recursion depth is memory as well: every nested call takes a frame on the thread stack, and recursion of depth n costs O(n) memory even without a single array.
cards/3/title: Logarithm: how many times you can halve
cards/3/body:
log₂ n is how many times you can halve n before 1 is left. It is also the number of doublings it takes to get from 1 to n. It grows very slowly: log₂ 10³ ≈ 10, log₂ 10⁶ ≈ 20, log₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30. The base is not written inside O: log₂ n and log₁₀ n differ by a constant factor.

O(log n) is an algorithm that discards half of the candidates at every step. The example is binary search in a sorted array: look at the middle; if it is less than the target, the answer is to the right and the left half is thrown away; if greater, the other way round. A million elements take at most 20 comparisons. In .NET this is Array.BinarySearch and List<T>.BinarySearch.

O(n log n) is doing a log n operation n times, or splitting the problem in half and merging the halves in O(n). That is how sorting works: Array.Sort is O(n log n), about 2·10⁷ comparisons for n = 10⁶. A common shape of a solution is “sort, then one pass”: O(n log n) + O(n) = O(n log n).
cards/4/q: What is the complexity of this code?
cards/4/explain: The outer loop runs n times. The inner one doubles j: 1, 2, 4, … — it reaches n in about log₂ n steps. Nested loops multiply: n · log n.
cards/4/wrong/1: The inner loop does not step through j one by one — j doubles, so it runs log₂ n times, not n.
cards/4/wrong/2: The inner loop is not O(1): its iteration count grows with n, if slowly.
cards/4/wrong/3: log n is just the inner loop, and it runs n times.
cards/5/body:
List<T> stores its elements in an array. While there is room, Add writes into the next slot — O(1). When the array is full, the list allocates a new one twice as large (the first holds 4 elements), copies everything over and only then adds. That insertion costs O(n).

Count n additions as a whole. Copies happen at sizes 4, 8, 16, …, and in total 4 + 8 + … + n/2 < n elements are copied. Together with the writes themselves that is fewer than 2n operations for n calls, so O(1) per call. This is amortized complexity: expensive operations are rare, and their cost is spread over the cheap ones. It is a guarantee for any sequence of operations, not a probability — do not confuse it with “on average” for a hash table, where the average is over the keys.

It is the geometric growth that makes it work: if the list grew by 10 elements at a time, there would be on the order of n²/20 copies — O(n) per call. If n is known in advance, set the capacity: new List<int>(n) — no reallocations at all. In Unity every reallocation is a new array, and the old one becomes garbage for the collector; in code that runs every frame, that shows.
cards/6/q: You add 1000 elements one by one to an empty List<int>. How many elements are copied in total during reallocations?
cards/6/options/1: About 500,000: every Add copies the whole list
cards/6/options/3: 0: List<T> appends at the end without copying
cards/6/explain: Capacity grows 4 → 8 → … → 1024, and every doubling copies the whole old array: 4 + 8 + … + 512 = 1020. That is less than 2n, which is why Add is amortized O(1).
cards/6/wrong/1: That would be the case if Add copied everything every time. A copy only happens when the array is full, and that gets rarer and rarer: capacity doubles.
cards/6/wrong/2: There are indeed 8 doublings (from 4 to 1024), but each one copies not one element but the whole old array.
cards/6/wrong/3: While there is room, yes. But when the array is full, a new one is needed and the old elements move into it.
cards/7/body:
The constraints in a problem statement are not a formality: they hint at which solution is expected. The rule of thumb is about 10⁸ simple operations per second. Where it comes from: a CPU runs on the order of 3·10⁹ cycles per second; a simple operation in a loop — a comparison, an addition, an array read — is a few instructions, and cache misses and branches cost more. In C# that comes out at 10⁸–10⁹ such operations per second, and 10⁸ is the safe estimate. With a 1–2 second limit, a solution has to fit into ~10⁸ operations.

Plug the maximum n into the complexity and compare with 10⁸:

n ≤ 10–11 → O(n!) — all permutations (10! ≈ 3.6·10⁶)
n ≤ 20 → O(2ⁿ) or O(2ⁿ·n) — all subsets (2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶)
n ≤ 500 → O(n³) (500³ ≈ 1.25·10⁸)
n ≤ 10⁴ → O(n²) (10⁸)
n ≤ 10⁶ → O(n log n) (≈ 2·10⁷)
n ≤ 10⁸ → O(n)
larger → O(log n) or O(1): such an n is no longer an array length but a number, and you need a formula or a binary search over values

The estimate is rough, but being off by 2–3× changes nothing: neighbouring rows differ by hundreds of times. If the statement has no constraints, ask: the answer “n up to a million” rules out O(n²) on the spot.

In a game the budget is tighter: a frame at 60 FPS is 16.7 ms, about 1.7·10⁶ simple operations for everything, the engine included. Checking all pairs of 1000 units — 5·10⁵ pairs — eats a noticeable share of the frame.
cards/8/q: The limit is 1 second. Which solutions fit? Select all.
cards/8/options/2: n ≤ 18, trying all subsets in O(2ⁿ·n)
cards/8/options/3: n ≤ 10⁶, an O(n log n) solution
cards/8/explain: 3000² ≈ 9·10⁶ — plenty of headroom. 2¹⁸ · 18 ≈ 4.7·10⁶ — same. 10⁶ · 20 = 2·10⁷ — fits. But 10⁵ squared is 10¹⁰, a hundred times over budget, and 300⁴ ≈ 8·10⁹ is eighty times over. The rule: plug in the maximum, compare with 10⁸.
cards/9/body:
The running example is Two Sum (LeetCode #1): find the indices of two numbers in nums that add up to target. Checking all pairs is n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, O(n²). But the inner loop looks for one specific value, target − x, from scratch every time. Remember everything seen so far in a Dictionary<int, int> “number → index”, and that lookup is O(1) on average, so one pass is enough: O(n) time, O(n) memory.

Why it is correct is explained by an invariant — a statement that holds before every iteration of the loop. Here: before step i the dictionary holds exactly nums[0..i−1]. If a pair (j, i) with j < i exists, then at step i its left element is already in the dictionary, so the pair is found. And so that a number does not find itself, we check first and insert after. The invariant is the main tool of this course: it proves the code correct, and it is what you say out loud in an interview.

The hash table unit covers this problem in detail. Here we care about cost: how many steps each solution takes.
cards/10/task: Step through the trace on [7, 3, 12, 1, 8, 4, 2, 6, 9, 15], target = 24. The pair sits at the very end — the worst case. Every step after the first is one dictionary lookup; count them. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next.
cards/10/goal/asks/0/q: The next x is 12, and the value to look for is 12 as well. What does the code do?
cards/10/goal/asks/0/explain: By the invariant the dictionary holds only what is to the left: 7 and 3. There is no 12 in it, so the code stores 12 → 2 and moves on. Had the insert come before the check, the number would have found itself and returned [2, 2].
cards/10/goal/asks/1/q: x = 15, looking for 9. What does the code do?
cards/10/goal/asks/1/explain: The 9 is in the dictionary at index 8: TryGetValue hands back j = 8, and the answer is { j, i } = { 8, 9 }. Ten lookups in total — one per element.
cards/11/q: The trace made 10 dictionary lookups. How many comparisons does checking all pairs i < j make on the same array before it reaches the pair (8, 9)?
cards/11/options/0: 45: it is the last pair, so it goes through all 10 · 9 / 2
cards/11/explain: The pair (8, 9) comes last in the order of the loops, so all n(n − 1)/2 = 45 pairs get checked. 45 versus 10 is not much yet. But for n = 10⁵ it is 5·10⁹ comparisons versus 10⁵ lookups: a gap of tens of thousands of times, even if a dictionary lookup costs 20–50 times more than a single comparison.
cards/11/wrong/1: 10 is the dictionary: one lookup per element. The brute force checks pairs, and there are on the order of n²/2 of them.
cards/11/wrong/2: n² includes the pairs (i, i) and both orientations of every pair. The loop with j = i + 1 checks each pair once: n(n − 1)/2.
cards/11/wrong/3: 10 · 9 counts (i, j) and (j, i) separately. The loop with j = i + 1 checks each pair once.
cards/12/title: When O(n²) beats O(n): constants and the cache
cards/12/body:
Big-O is about growth, not about the time at a particular n. A Dictionary lookup is a hash, a modulo, a walk along a chain and an Equals: from a few to tens of nanoseconds, depending on the runtime and the key type, versus a fraction of a nanosecond to compare neighbouring array elements. So for 8–16 elements a linear scan of an array often beats a dictionary, and O(n log n) with a small constant can outrun O(n) with a large one.

The second constant is memory. An array is contiguous, and the CPU pulls it into the cache in blocks. Nodes of a list or a tree are scattered across the managed heap, and every hop can cost a cache miss — on the order of a hundred nanoseconds. The same O(n) traversal of an array and of a LinkedList<T> differs several times over.

In an interview you name the asymptotics first and, if asked about real speed, the constants: “for small n the linear scan wins, but at n = 10⁵ the dictionary is orders of magnitude faster”.
cards/12/deep:
Formally. f(n) = O(g(n)) if f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀ for some constant c: it is an upper bound. Θ is a tight bound (from above and below), Ω a lower one. In interviews “O” is usually meant as Θ: “checking all pairs is O(n²)” means “grows like n²”. Formally O(n²) is also true of a linear algorithm, but nobody answers that way.

Amortization and the spike of a single operation. Amortized O(1) for List<T>.Add does not stop an individual call from costing O(n): with 10⁶ int elements one doubling copies 4 MB. On a server nobody notices; in a game it is a spike in the frame graph. Hence the rule for hot code: capacity up front (new List<T>(n), the Capacity property), collections in fields and Clear() instead of new.

Why doubling. Any factor greater than 1 works: growing by a factor of k gives fewer than n/(k − 1) copies for n inserts. In .NET List<T>, Stack<T> and Queue<T> double, and Dictionary grows to a prime no smaller than twice its size. Collections never shrink on their own: Clear() keeps the capacity, and TrimExcess() gives the memory back.

Several parameters. A graph is O(V + E), two strings are O(n·m), “the best k out of n” is O(n log k). Do not reduce everything to one letter: “O(n log k), with k ≪ n” is a senior answer.
cards/13/q: Match the constraint with the affordable complexity (a 1–2 second limit).
